body: A churchwarden is up a stepladder in a vestry cupboard on a Saturday morning, taking down box files nobody has opened since before she was born, because the roof fund needs the room. In one of them is a minute book bound in black cloth. She sits down on the second step of the ladder with it open on her knee and reads a paragraph in which the elders record, unanimously, that no wireless set is to be installed in the church hall, on the grounds that it would keep the young people at home. Underneath, in a different hand and a much later ink, somebody has written a time, a wavelength, and the words Sunday service, relay. She puts the book on the pile to keep.

That cupboard holds the whole argument twice over, in one book, in two hands. It is not a story about foolish men. Both entries were made by people trying to protect the same thing, and the only difference between them was thirty years of finding out what a wireless actually did.

Print was going to put Scripture into the hands of people unqualified to read it. Radio was going to empty the pews. Television was going to turn faith into a performance. The internet was going to dissolve the local church into a screen.

The argument arrives in a new costume each time, but underneath it is always the same argument, and it is always about mediation. Something new has got in between the believer and the thing itself — between the reader and the priest who used to read for him, between the congregant and the room, between the worshipper and the actual bodies he is supposed to be worshipping alongside. That is a serious objection rather than a silly one, because this faith is incarnational and keeps insisting on bodies in rooms. A medium that lets a person have the shape of the thing without the substance of it is a genuine danger, and every generation that raised the alarm was pointing at something that existed.

This band is that argument arriving again, in about the plainest form it has ever taken. It runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70, carries 121 assigned frequencies with 46 live at this moment, and every song on it was composed by a machine against a brief written by a person.

Saying that out loud costs something, and the cheaper option was available. It would be easy enough to say nothing about how the music is made, and a great many listeners would never think to ask. It is said plainly instead, along with the failure modes, because the alternative is to leave the objection for somebody else to make later and worse. None of the old fears was stupid, and this is the part usually skipped: each one named a real failure mode, and each failure mode duly arrived. There is bad television preaching. There is a version of online church that has become a substitute rather than a supplement. The fears were right about the risk and wrong about the conclusion, every single time.

Being late has a cost, and it has always been the same cost. There is a stretch during which the new medium is shaped entirely by people with no interest in the Kingdom, and by the time the Church arrives the room has already been furnished — the conventions set, the formats fixed, the vocabulary meaning what somebody else decided it should mean. Nobody is being malicious. It simply happens while the argument is still going on in the vestry.

So the safeguards here are structural rather than promised, which is the only kind worth anything. A frequency is permanent and cannot be reassigned when a station stops being fashionable. The schedule is published before it airs rather than assembled behind the listener. Every track stands on a passage that can be gone to and read, attached to a permanent identifier rather than to a title somebody could quietly edit. And nothing reaches the air unread by a person.
None of which touches the strongest form of the objection, which deserves to be put at its full strength rather than its weakest.

It runs like this. Tools are not neutral. A medium does not merely carry what you put into it; it forms the people using it, in its own image, whatever the content happens to be. Television turned the sermon into a performance not because preachers were vain but because that is what a camera does to a man standing still. On that reading, taking up a new tool for the gospel is not a decision about content at all — you may put the purest possible material through it and be reshaped by the machinery regardless. That is the serious version, and it is largely true. The difficulty is what is supposed to follow from it, because abstention has never exempted anybody from a medium. It only removes them from it.
Staying out has not once kept a medium away from the pews. It has only kept the Church out of the medium.

A boy of seventeen has a station on in his room at half past eleven at night, on headphones, because a friend sent him a link during a dull afternoon and he never got round to closing the tab. He has not been to church since he was eleven and has no intention of going. He is not listening properly; he is doing something else and it is on. Over a fortnight one particular song keeps coming back, and he reads the passage underneath it once, standing up, to find out whether it really says anything as strange as it sounds. It is stranger. On the Tuesday he asks his mother a question about Job at breakfast, and she puts the kettle down.

Nobody preached at him and nobody invited him anywhere. A medium his church has not yet decided whether to approve of carried a chapter of the Old Testament into his bedroom while he was thinking about something else entirely.

The failure mode of this particular tool is real and it can be named without hedging. It is a flood — an unlimited supply of plausible religious material that nobody has read, songs that sound true and mean nothing, devotional text produced by the yard. It is already happening. The worst of it is not heresy but weightlessness: words with nobody behind them, teaching people slowly that language about God is cheap.

That is an argument for standards, not for abstention, and the press settled this one already. The printing press produced heresy in industrial quantities, and the answer was never less printing. It was better printing, done carefully, by people willing to put their names to it. The flood is coming either way. The only question actually on the table is whether anything in it will have been made by somebody who checked.

So the risk in front of the Church now is not the risk of using the tools, and it never has been. It is the old risk in its usual costume: arriving late to a room somebody else has already furnished, and then spending twenty years working in their arrangement of it. The fears kept being right about the danger. They kept being wrong about what to do next, and it was the same wrong answer every time.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

What is on this dial comes in four kinds, and it helps to know they are there. There is music, which is most of the band — worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe: clean, warm, and playable in a room with children in it. And there are 40 international frequencies carrying 29 languages besides English, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. One dial, four kinds, and no menu to work your way through.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 313.80 — The Ancient Paths. It takes its name from the line in Jeremiah about standing at the crossroads and asking for the old ways, and it makes this article’s point without saying a word about it: Amir’s maqam-based Middle Eastern worship and acoustic lament, the oldest-sounding music anywhere on this band, carried by the newest tool in the room. It sounds like home to an Arabic-speaking believer and like nothing else on earth to everybody else. Put it on and the question of whether the Church ought to touch a new medium goes oddly quiet, because what comes out of it is older than every fear in that minute book.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — the site is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than a rebuttal. You are allowed to keep the objection; the elders in that vestry were not wrong to have one, and the ones who came after them did not cross the first entry out. They simply wrote a time and a wavelength underneath it. Put HM 313.80 on this afternoon while you are doing something else, and let it run for a week of ordinary days. Then decide what to write in the book.
